```{python}
# | echo: false
# All reported values are read from training_stats.json, which is regenerated
# end to end by:
#     python reproduce.py                  # descriptives, mixed models, agreement
#     python extract_manuscript_stats.py   # SPM, progression, baseline, counts
#     python extract_validity_stats.py     # velocity phase, agreement by dataset
#     python extract_stats_addendum.py     # Welch df, terminal contrasts
# No number below is typed by hand. If a value is not in the JSON it does not
# appear in the text.
import json

from jhamon_training.pathutils import RESULTS_TRAINING_PATH

with open(RESULTS_TRAINING_PATH / "training_stats.json") as f:
    S = json.load(f)
with open(RESULTS_TRAINING_PATH / "manuscript_stats_detail.json") as f:
    D = json.load(f)


def p(key, *, eq=True):
    """Format a p value: '< 0.001' below that, otherwise three decimals."""
    v = float(S[key]) if isinstance(key, str) else float(key)
    if v < 0.001:
        return "*p* < 0.001" if eq else "< 0.001"
    return f"*p* = {v:.3f}" if eq else f"= {v:.3f}"


def pv(v):
    """Same, for a raw number rather than a key."""
    return "< 0.001" if float(v) < 0.001 else f"= {float(v):.3f}"


def ms(mean_key, sd_key, nd=1):
    return f"{S[mean_key]:.{nd}f} ± {S[sd_key]:.{nd}f}"


def sg(key, nd=2):
    """Signed value, with negative zero normalised so it never prints '-0.00'."""
    v = float(S[key]) if isinstance(key, str) else float(key)
    if abs(v) < 0.5 * 10**-nd:
        v = 0.0
    return f"{v:+.{nd}f}"


def ci(low_key, high_key, nd=2, sign=False):
    lo, hi = S[low_key], S[high_key]
    fmt = f"+.{nd}f" if sign else f".{nd}f"
    return f"{lo:{fmt}}, {hi:{fmt}}"


def cluster(prefix, n):
    """One SPM cluster as 'start–end%' plus its cluster-level p."""
    lo, hi = S[f"{prefix}_c{n}_start"], S[f"{prefix}_c{n}_end"]
    return f"{lo:.1f}–{hi:.1f}%", pv(S[f"{prefix}_c{n}_p"])


# Data completeness. All participants completed all 15 sessions; the missing
# cells are recordings that were not captured or retained (technical failure
# during acquisition), NOT missed training sessions.
n_par = S["lmm_n_participants"]
n_cells = S["lmm_n_cells"]
n_possible = n_par * 15
n_missing = n_possible - n_cells
pct_complete = f"{100 * n_cells / n_possible:.0f}"

# Verified 2026-07-27 by rebuilding the (par x session) grid from the caches.
n_missing_nh, n_missing_ik = 10, 2   # missing recordings, per group
n_affected = 9                       # participants with >=1 missing recording
n_complete_case = 18                 # what a complete-case ANOVA would retain

# The five discrete outcomes, in the order they are reported.
DVS = [
    ("angle_at_peak_torque", "knee angle at peak torque", "°", 1),
    ("peak_torque", "peak torque", "N·m", 1),
    ("mean_torque", "mean torque", "N·m", 1),
    ("knee_ROM", "knee range of motion", "°", 1),
    ("knee_v_mean", "mean knee angular velocity", "°/s", 1),
]
d = {}
for dv, _label, _unit, nd in DVS:
    d[f"{dv}_nh"] = ms(f"lmm_{dv}_desc_nh_mean", f"lmm_{dv}_desc_nh_sd", nd)
    d[f"{dv}_ik"] = ms(f"lmm_{dv}_desc_ik_mean", f"lmm_{dv}_desc_ik_sd", nd)
    d[f"{dv}_est"] = f'{S[f"lmm_{dv}_nhmik_est"]:+.2f}'
    d[f"{dv}_ci"] = ci(f"lmmt_{dv}_ci_low", f"lmmt_{dv}_ci_high", sign=True)
    d[f"{dv}_t"] = f'{S[f"lmmt_{dv}_t"]:.2f}'
    d[f"{dv}_p"] = pv(S[f"lmmt_{dv}_p"])
    for eff in ["group", "time", "interaction"]:
        d[f"{dv}_{eff}_chi2"] = f'{S[f"lmm_{dv}_{eff}_chi2"]:.1f}'
        d[f"{dv}_{eff}_df"] = S[f"lmm_{dv}_{eff}_df"]
        d[f"{dv}_{eff}_p"] = pv(S[f"lmm_{dv}_{eff}_p"])
```

# Statistical analysis

## Software and reporting conventions

All analyses were performed in Python 3.9.6. Descriptive statistics, agreement
analyses and *t*-tests used SciPy 1.13.1 (Virtanen et al., 2020); linear mixed
models used `statsmodels` 0.14.6 (Seabold & Perktold, 2010); one-dimensional
statistical parametric mapping used `spm1d` 0.4.53 (Pataky, 2012); descriptive
summaries used `pingouin` 0.5.5 (Vallat, 2018). Descriptive data are presented
as mean ± standard deviation (SD), with the unit of analysis stated in each
case, and model effects as the estimate with its 95% confidence interval (CI).
The significance level was set at α = 0.05. All code and the complete set of
reported statistics are archived with the manuscript, and every value reported
below is regenerated from the archived data by a single documented command.

## Analysed data and data reduction

Two nested populations of repetitions are distinguished throughout, because
they answer different questions and are not interchangeable.

*All repetitions performed* comprises every repetition recorded during the
intervention (`{python} S["reps_all_total"]` repetitions;
`{python} S["reps_all_nh"]` NH in `{python} S["reps_all_nh_sets"]` sets and
`{python} S["reps_all_ik"]` IK in `{python} S["reps_all_ik_sets"]` sets). This
is the population the standardization procedure actually targeted, since the
cumulative work criterion that terminated each isokinetic set was applied to
every repetition performed, and it is therefore the population used for the
descriptive summaries and for the agreement analyses that evaluate the
standardization.

*Analysed repetitions* comprises `{python} S["reps_analysed_total"]`
repetitions remaining after three exclusions: (i) sets that were not part of
the matched prescription grid, (ii) individual participant–session–set
recordings identified as technically invalid during data collection, and (iii)
a quality-control window retaining only repetitions with a mean knee angular
velocity between 10 and 35 °·s^-1^.

Criterion (iii) filters on a variable that is also a reported outcome, and its
effect is not symmetric between groups, so it is quantified here rather than
asserted to be harmless. Applied after criteria (i) and (ii), which are protocol
facts known independently of any measurement, it removed
`{python} S["qc_nh_fast"] + S["qc_nh_slow"]`
of `{python} S["qc_nh_n"]` NH repetitions
(`{python} f'{S["qc_nh_removed_pct"]:.1f}'`%), of which
`{python} S["qc_nh_fast"]` came from the fast tail at speeds not physiologically
attainable during a Nordic descent and `{python} S["qc_nh_slow"]` from the slow
tail; and `{python} S["qc_ik_fast"] + S["qc_ik_slow"]` of
`{python} S["qc_ik_n"]` IK repetitions
(`{python} f'{S["qc_ik_removed_pct"]:.1f}'`%), all from the slow tail, since an
isokinetic movement cannot exceed its programmed speed. Trimming the Nordic fast
tail and the isokinetic slow tail moves the two group means towards each other
(NH `{python} sg("qc_nh_mean_shift")` °·s^-1^, IK
`{python} sg("qc_ik_mean_shift")` °·s^-1^; NH − IK gap
`{python} f'{S["qc_gap_before"]:.2f}'` → `{python} f'{S["qc_gap_after"]:.2f}'`
°·s^-1^) and is therefore **anti-conservative** for a claim that the two
modalities were velocity-matched. The agreement analyses that evaluate the
standardization are accordingly reported on all repetitions performed, with the
analysed subset given as a sensitivity analysis.

The three analyses draw on different populations, which is stated here because
no single repetition count describes them all. The between-modality whole-curve
comparison used all `{python} S["reps_all_total"]` recorded repetitions,
averaged to one curve per participant. The mixed models and the
session-by-session whole-curve comparisons used the three repetitions of highest
peak torque in each participant × session cell.

For the discrete outcomes, the three repetitions with the highest peak torque
within each participant and training session were averaged, yielding one value
per participant × session combination. The selection criterion is peak torque
and the pool from which those three repetitions are drawn grows across the
programme as sets and repetitions are added; both are stated here because the
mean of an extreme order statistic increases with pool size, and this
contributes to, without accounting for, the observed time effects.

## Baseline comparison

Pre-intervention maximal voluntary isometric knee-flexion torque — the quantity
by which the isokinetic work prescription was individually scaled in Equation 1
— was compared between groups with an independent-samples Welch *t*-test, with
Hedges' *g* as the effect size. Participants completed one to three
familiarisation sessions; the highest value across a participant's sessions was
used, and the conclusion was verified to be unchanged under a mean-across-
sessions and a last-session rule. One NH participant lacked a usable passive
trial for gravity correction and is therefore excluded from this comparison
only (NH *n* = `{python} S["mvif_max_nh_n"]`, IK *n* =
`{python} S["mvif_max_ik_n"]`); all `{python} n_par` participants contribute to
the mixed models and the between-modality whole-curve comparison. The
session-by-session progression comparisons are paired and therefore use only
participants with both sessions recorded (9–13 per contrast).

## Whole-curve analysis of the mechanical patterns

Torque and knee angular velocity were time-normalised to 101 points across the
eccentric phase of each repetition and compared between modalities using
one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping (SPM1D; Pataky, 2012). Curves
are expressed as a percentage of the repetition rather than of knee angle;
because the two modalities traverse a comparable total range of motion but at
different instantaneous rates, matched percentages do not correspond to
identical knee angles, and the corresponding angular ranges are reported
alongside each result.

Between-modality differences were tested with a two-sample SPM{*t*} statistic
computed on **one curve per participant** (`{python} S["spm_torque_paravg_n_nh"]`
NH versus `{python} S["spm_torque_paravg_n_ik"]` IK), obtained by averaging each
participant's repetitions across all sessions. This unit of analysis is stated
explicitly because averaging within participant is what makes the observations
independent: treating each participant × session curve as a separate
observation would inflate the residual degrees of freedom approximately
fifteen-fold.

Within-group changes across the intervention were tested by comparing each
subsequent session against the first with a paired SPM{*t*} statistic (14
comparisons per group). For each test the critical threshold *t*\* was defined
using random field theory, which controls the family-wise error rate across the
101 points of a single curve but not across the 14 session comparisons; the
per-comparison α was therefore Bonferroni-corrected to
`{python} f'{S["prog_alpha_bonferroni"]:.4f}'` (0.05/`{python} S["prog_n_comparisons"]`).
Because that correction is conservative for a family of positively correlated,
time-ordered contrasts sharing a common reference session, the uncorrected
results are also reported. Supra-threshold clusters and their cluster-level
probabilities are reported for every test.

## Repetitions and mechanical work

The number of repetitions performed per set and the mechanical work performed
per repetition were compared between modalities with independent-samples Welch
*t*-tests, with Hedges' *g* as the effect size. In both cases the unit of
analysis is the participant: each participant contributed a single mean, and
the tests were computed on `{python} S["workrep_nh_n"]` NH and
`{python} S["workrep_ik_n"]` IK values. Repetition-level tests on the full set
of `{python} S["reps_all_total"]` repetitions are not reported, because
repetitions within a participant are not independent observations. Repetition
counts are compared as achieved-versus-achieved; comparisons of achieved
isokinetic counts against the prescribed Nordic count are not reported, since
the NH group completed 92% of the prescription and such a comparison
understates the difference.

## Validity of the work- and velocity-standardization

The validity of the standardization was evaluated with Bland–Altman analyses of
the two quantities the procedure equated: total mechanical work per set, and
mean angular velocity.

Because NH and IK were **between-participant** groups, there is no
participant-to-participant correspondence and a conventional paired
Bland–Altman analysis on individual data would be meaningless. What the
procedure paired was the *prescription*: the target work for a given set of a
given session was derived from the NH group mean for that same session × set
cell, and the dynamometer velocity for that cell was programmed to the NH group
mean for that cell. The unit of analysis is therefore the **session × set
cell**, of which there are `{python} S["bav_all_work_n_pairs"]` complete pairs,
each comparing the NH group mean against the IK group mean for the same cell,
with the difference taken as NH − IK. For work, repetitions were summed within
participant and then averaged across the participants of the group; for
velocity, the mean was taken across all repetitions in the cell.

For each quantity we report the mean bias with its 95% CI, the 95% limits of
agreement (bias ± 1.96 SD of the differences) with their CIs, the bias as a
percentage of the grand mean, Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC)
with its CI, a test for proportional bias (ordinary least-squares regression of
the difference on the mean), and a Shapiro–Wilk test of the differences. Where
proportional bias was significant, regression-based limits of agreement are
reported alongside the fixed limits. Two distinct confidence intervals are
reported and are not interchangeable: the cell-level interval describes how
reproducibly the standardization hit its target from one session × set cell to
the next, whereas the between-group difference and its interval are computed
with the **participant** as the unit of analysis and are the appropriate basis
for any statement about the two groups. Equivalence is not argued from a
non-significant test; it is argued from the magnitude of the bias relative to
the measured quantity, together with the limits of agreement.

The velocity comparison requires one further definition, and it is deliberately
**asymmetric between the two modalities**, so it is set out in full here.

What the procedure prescribed was a single constant angular velocity per set,
equal to the Nordic group's mean angular velocity over the whole range of motion
for that set. Evaluating whether that prescription was met therefore means
comparing the Nordic whole-range mean — the quantity that defined the target —
against the constant velocity the dynamometer actually delivered. The
dynamometer necessarily accelerates the limb from rest at the start of the range
of motion and decelerates it to rest at the end, and both ramps fall inside the
recorded repetition; they are properties of the apparatus and were not part of
the prescription. Isokinetic velocity was accordingly quantified over the
**constant-velocity phase**, defined as the samples whose absolute angular
velocity reached at least 95% of that repetition's peak. Across the
`{python} S["velphase_n_reps"]` isokinetic repetitions this phase spanned the
median interval
`{python} f'{S["velphase_start_pct_median"]:.0f}'`–`{python} f'{S["velphase_end_pct_median"]:.0f}'`%
of the repetition, and including the two ramps lowered the mean velocity from
`{python} f'{S["velphase_ik_plateau_mean"]:.2f}'` to
`{python} f'{S["velphase_ik_window_mean"]:.2f}'` °·s^-1^
(`{python} f'{S["velphase_ramp_cost_pct"]:.0f}'`%). The value is insensitive to
the threshold (`{python} f'{S["velphase_p90_mean"]:.2f}'`,
`{python} f'{S["velphase_ik_plateau_mean"]:.2f}'` and
`{python} f'{S["velphase_p98_mean"]:.2f}'` °·s^-1^ at 90%, 95% and 98% of peak
respectively, and `{python} f'{S["velphase_ik_mid_mean"]:.2f}'` °·s^-1^ over a
fixed 25–75% window).

No equivalent trimming was applied to the Nordic repetitions, and the reason is
empirical rather than conventional: a Nordic descent has no constant-velocity
phase to isolate. Applying the identical 95%-of-peak rule to the Nordic curves
selects a median of `{python} S["velphase_nh_p95_width_median"]` of the 101
sample points and returns `{python} f'{S["velphase_nh_p95_mean"]:.1f}'` °·s^-1^,
because the Nordic profile accelerates monotonically to the end of its window
rather than plateauing; a fixed 25–75% window returns
`{python} f'{S["velphase_nh_mid2575_mean"]:.2f}'` °·s^-1^, which measures a
different part of an accelerating ramp than the same window measures in the
isokinetic group. Neither is a like-for-like quantity, whereas the Nordic
whole-range mean is precisely the quantity the isokinetic target was derived
from. The comparison reported below is therefore between the Nordic whole-range
mean and the isokinetic constant-velocity phase, and it should be read as a test
of whether the prescribed velocity was delivered — not as a claim that the two
modalities imposed equivalent velocity profiles, which the whole-curve analysis
shows they did not. The isokinetic whole-window value is reported alongside so
that the effect of this choice is explicit.

## Discrete outcomes across training sessions

Mechanical data were unavailable for `{python} n_missing` of the
`{python} n_possible` participant × session combinations owing to technical
failures during data acquisition. A conventional repeated-measures analysis of
variance would have excluded the `{python} n_affected` affected participants
listwise and reduced the sample from `{python} n_par` to
`{python} n_complete_case`. Data were therefore analysed with linear mixed
models, which accommodate unbalanced designs and use all available observations
(Cnaan et al., 1997; Gueorguieva & Krystal, 2004), retaining all
`{python} n_par` participants. Missingness was concentrated in the NH group
(`{python} n_missing_nh` of 195 NH cells versus `{python} n_missing_ik` of 210
IK cells), consistent with the heavier NH instrumentation, and was unrelated to
the measured outcomes; because training group is a fixed effect in every model,
the data are treated as missing at random.

Each outcome was modelled with training group (NH, IK), training session (15
levels, treated as a categorical factor) and their interaction as fixed effects,
and a random intercept for participant. Sum-to-zero contrast coding was used so
that the group and session tests represent main effects averaged over the levels
of the other factor. Models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood, and
main effects and the interaction were tested with omnibus Wald chi-square tests.
The between-group effect is reported as the estimated marginal difference
(NH − IK), averaged equally across training sessions, with a 95% CI based on the
*t* distribution with `{python} S["lmmt_df"]` degrees of freedom, that being the
number of participants minus two rather than the number of observations. Two
limitations of this specification are acknowledged: the omnibus Wald tests are
asymptotic and are referred to a chi-square distribution, which is
anti-conservative for the between-participant group effect at this sample size;
and a single residual and a single random-intercept variance are estimated for
both groups, although the isokinetic constraint makes the between-participant
variance in velocity and range of motion substantially smaller in the IK group.

# Results

## Participants and data yield

All `{python} n_par` participants (`{python} S["lmm_n_nh"]` NH,
`{python} S["lmm_n_ik"]` IK) completed the full 15-session training programme.
Mechanical data were successfully recorded for `{python} n_cells` of the
`{python} n_possible` participant × session combinations
(`{python} pct_complete`%); the `{python} n_missing` missing recordings were due
to technical failures during data acquisition (`{python} n_missing_nh` NH,
`{python} n_missing_ik` IK), affecting `{python} n_affected` participants.

The two groups did not differ at baseline in maximal voluntary isometric
knee-flexion torque (NH `{python} ms("mvif_max_nh_mean", "mvif_max_nh_sd")` N·m,
*n* = `{python} S["mvif_max_nh_n"]`; IK
`{python} ms("mvif_max_ik_mean", "mvif_max_ik_sd")` N·m, *n* =
`{python} S["mvif_max_ik_n"]`; *t* = `{python} f'{S["mvif_max_t"]:.2f}'`,
*p* = `{python} f'{S["mvif_max_p"]:.3f}'`, *g* =
`{python} f'{S["mvif_max_g"]:.2f}'`), which is the condition under which the
group-mean scaling of Equation 1 is appropriate. The same conclusion was
obtained using the mean across familiarisation sessions
(*p* = `{python} f'{S["mvif_mean_p"]:.3f}'`) or the last session
(*p* = `{python} f'{S["mvif_last_p"]:.3f}'`).

A total of `{python} S["reps_all_total"]` repetitions were recorded
(`{python} S["reps_all_nh"]` NH, `{python} S["reps_all_ik"]` IK), of which
`{python} S["reps_analysed_total"]` entered the whole-curve and mixed-model
analyses.

## Effect of training modality on the mechanical patterns

The two modalities loaded the knee in opposite regions of the range of motion
(Figure 3). Between-group SPM{*t*} analysis of the torque curves
(*t*\*(`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_df"]:.1f}'`) =
`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_tstar"]:.3f}'`) identified two
supra-threshold clusters. Isokinetic torque exceeded Nordic torque over the
first `{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c1_end"]:.1f}'`% of the repetition
(`{python} cluster("spm_torque_paravg", 1)[0]`, cluster-level
*p* `{python} cluster("spm_torque_paravg", 1)[1]`), spanning
`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c1_nh_angle_start"]:.1f}'`° to
`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c1_nh_angle_end"]:.1f}'`° of knee flexion in
the NH group and `{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c1_ik_angle_start"]:.1f}'`°
to `{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c1_ik_angle_end"]:.1f}'`° in the IK group;
within that cluster mean torque was
`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c1_nh_value"]:.1f}'` N·m in the NH group
against `{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c1_ik_value"]:.1f}'` N·m in the IK
group (`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c1_pct_diff"]:+.1f}'`%). Nordic torque
exceeded isokinetic torque over the final quarter
(`{python} cluster("spm_torque_paravg", 2)[0]`, *p*
`{python} cluster("spm_torque_paravg", 2)[1]`;
`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_nh_angle_start"]:.1f}'`°–`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_nh_angle_end"]:.1f}'`°
NH and `{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_ik_angle_start"]:.1f}'`°–`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_ik_angle_end"]:.1f}'`°
IK), where mean torque was
`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_nh_value"]:.1f}'` N·m against
`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_ik_value"]:.1f}'` N·m
(`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_pct_diff"]:+.1f}'`%).

Angular velocity showed a correspondingly opposite pattern
(*t*\*(`{python} f'{S["spm_velocity_paravg_df"]:.1f}'`) =
`{python} f'{S["spm_velocity_paravg_tstar"]:.3f}'`). Isokinetic velocity
exceeded Nordic velocity over the first 70% of the movement
(`{python} cluster("spm_velocity_paravg", 2)[0]`, *p*
`{python} cluster("spm_velocity_paravg", 2)[1]`;
`{python} f'{S["spm_velocity_paravg_c2_ik_value"]:.1f}'` °·s^-1^ in the IK group
against `{python} f'{S["spm_velocity_paravg_c2_nh_value"]:.1f}'` °·s^-1^ in the
NH group), and Nordic velocity exceeded isokinetic velocity over the final fifth
(`{python} cluster("spm_velocity_paravg", 3)[0]`, *p*
`{python} cluster("spm_velocity_paravg", 3)[1]`;
`{python} f'{S["spm_velocity_paravg_c3_nh_value"]:.1f}'` °·s^-1^ in the NH group
against `{python} f'{S["spm_velocity_paravg_c3_ik_value"]:.1f}'` °·s^-1^ in the
IK group), where the
Nordic descent accelerates towards the horizontal while the dynamometer is
decelerating the limb at the end of its range of motion. A further cluster
confined to the first `{python} f'{S["spm_velocity_paravg_c1_end"]:.1f}'`% of
the repetition (*p* = `{python} f'{S["spm_velocity_paravg_c1_p"]:.4f}'`, a single
sample point wide) reflects the instant at which the dynamometer had not yet begun to move the limb
and is not interpreted further.

The angular ranges above make explicit that a matched percentage of the
repetition does not correspond to a matched knee angle: the final quarter of the
repetition covers
`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_nh_angle_start"] - S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_nh_angle_end"]:.1f}'`°
of knee extension in the NH group but only
`{python} f'{S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_ik_angle_start"] - S["spm_torque_paravg_c2_ik_angle_end"]:.1f}'`°
in the IK group, because the Nordic descent accelerates while the isokinetic
movement does not.

These divergent profiles are a direct consequence of the two resistance types:
the isokinetic dynamometer imposes an accommodating resistance at a constant
angular velocity from the outset, whereas the Nordic descent is
gravity-dependent, so torque rises and velocity accelerates as the lever arm
lengthens towards the horizontal.

## Repetitions and mechanical work

To reach the same prescribed work per set, participants in the IK group
performed `{python} f'{S["reps_all_perset_ik"]:.2f}'` ±
`{python} f'{S["reps_all_perset_ik_sd"]:.2f}'` repetitions per set compared with
`{python} f'{S["reps_all_perset_nh"]:.2f}'` ±
`{python} f'{S["reps_all_perset_nh_sd"]:.2f}'` in the NH group, a difference of
`{python} f'{S["reps_all_perset_diff"]:.2f}'` repetitions per set (95% CI
[`{python} ci("reps_all_perset_ci_low", "reps_all_perset_ci_high")`];
*t*(`{python} f'{S["reps_all_perset_df"]:.1f}'`) =
`{python} f'{S["reps_all_perset_t"]:.2f}'`, *p*
`{python} pv(S["reps_all_perset_p"])`, *g* =
`{python} f'{S["reps_all_perset_g"]:.2f}'`; Figure 4A). The gap was present from the
first session (IK `{python} f'{S["reps_all_tr1_perset_ik"]:.2f}'` versus NH
`{python} f'{S["reps_all_tr1_perset_nh"]:.2f}'` repetitions per set) and of a
similar magnitude at the fifteenth (IK
`{python} f'{S["reps_all_tr15_perset_ik"]:.2f}'` versus NH
`{python} f'{S["reps_all_tr15_perset_nh"]:.2f}'`); both groups' counts rose
across the programme because the prescription itself progressed from five to
eight repetitions per set.

The additional repetitions were required because each isokinetic repetition
delivered less work. Mechanical work per repetition was greater in the NH group
(`{python} ms("workrep_nh_mean", "workrep_nh_sd")` J versus
`{python} ms("workrep_ik_mean", "workrep_ik_sd")` J; mean difference
`{python} f'{S["workrep_diff"]:.1f}'` J, 95% CI
[`{python} ci("workrep_ci_low", "workrep_ci_high", nd=1)`];
*t*(`{python} f'{S["workrep_df"]:.1f}'`) = `{python} f'{S["workrep_t"]:.2f}'`,
*p* `{python} pv(S["workrep_p"])`, *g* = `{python} f'{S["workrep_g"]:.2f}'`;
Figure 4B). Total work per set was consequently similar between groups
(`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_par_nh_mean"]:.1f}'` ±
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_par_nh_sd"]:.1f}'` J versus
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_par_ik_mean"]:.1f}'` ±
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_par_ik_sd"]:.1f}'` J, participant means;
Figure 4C), which is quantified in the following section.

## Validity of the work- and velocity-standardization

**Mechanical work per set.** Across the
`{python} S["bav_all_work_n_pairs"]` session × set cells, the mean NH − IK
difference was `{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_bias"]:+.1f}'` J (95% CI
[`{python} ci("bav_all_work_bias_ci_low", "bav_all_work_bias_ci_high", nd=1, sign=True)`],
*p* = `{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_bias_p"]:.3f}'`), equivalent to
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_pct_bias"]:+.2f}'`% of the
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_grand_mean"]:.1f}'` J grand mean, with 95% limits of
agreement of `{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_loa_low"]:.1f}'` (95% CI
[`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_loa_low_ci_low"]:.1f}'`,
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_loa_low_ci_high"]:.1f}'`]) to
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_loa_high"]:+.1f}'` J (95% CI
[`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_loa_high_ci_low"]:.1f}'`,
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_loa_high_ci_high"]:.1f}'`]), i.e.
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_pct_loa_low"]:.2f}'`% to
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_pct_loa_high"]:+.2f}'`%, and a concordance
correlation coefficient of `{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_ccc"]:.3f}'` (95% CI
[`{python} ci("bav_all_work_ccc_ci_low", "bav_all_work_ccc_ci_high", nd=3)`];
Pearson *r* = `{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_pearson_r"]:.3f}'`). The differences
were normally distributed (Shapiro–Wilk *p* =
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_shapiro_p"]:.3f}'`). A proportional bias was present
(slope `{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_prop_slope"]:.3f}'`, *p*
`{python} pv(S["bav_all_work_prop_p"])`): the NH − IK difference increased with
the magnitude of the work performed, so the near-zero average masks a small
negative bias in the lowest-load cells and a small positive bias in the highest.
The corresponding regression-based limits of agreement are
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_reg_intercept"]:.1f}'` +
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_reg_slope"]:.3f}'` × mean ±
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_reg_half_width"]:.1f}'` J. Taking the participant
rather than the cell as the unit of analysis, the between-group difference in
work per set was `{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_par_bias"]:+.1f}'` J (95% CI
[`{python} ci("bav_all_work_par_ci_low", "bav_all_work_par_ci_high", nd=1, sign=True)`];
*t*(`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_par_df"]:.1f}'`) =
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_par_t"]:.2f}'`, *p* =
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_par_p"]:.3f}'`, *g* =
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_work_par_g"]:.2f}'`).

**Angular velocity.** Comparing the Nordic whole-range mean with the isokinetic
constant-velocity phase, the mean NH − IK difference was
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_bias"]:+.2f}'` °·s^-1^ (95% CI
[`{python} ci("bav_all_viso_bias_ci_low", "bav_all_viso_bias_ci_high", sign=True)`],
*p* `{python} pv(S["bav_all_viso_bias_p"])`),
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_pct_bias"]:+.2f}'`% of the
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_grand_mean"]:.2f}'` °·s^-1^ grand mean, with limits
of agreement of `{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_loa_low"]:.2f}'` (95% CI
[`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_loa_low_ci_low"]:.2f}'`,
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_loa_low_ci_high"]:.2f}'`]) to
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_loa_high"]:+.2f}'` °·s^-1^ (95% CI
[`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_loa_high_ci_low"]:.2f}'`,
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_loa_high_ci_high"]:.2f}'`]), i.e.
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_pct_loa_low"]:.2f}'`% to
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_pct_loa_high"]:+.2f}'`%, and a concordance
correlation coefficient of `{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_ccc"]:.3f}'` (95% CI
[`{python} ci("bav_all_viso_ccc_ci_low", "bav_all_viso_ccc_ci_high", nd=3)`]).
No proportional bias was detected (slope
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_prop_slope"]:.3f}'`, *p* =
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_prop_p"]:.3f}'`). The differences departed from
normality (Shapiro–Wilk *p* =
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_shapiro_p"]:.3f}'`), so the fixed limits above
should be read as approximate. Taking the participant as the unit of analysis,
the between-group difference was
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_par_bias"]:+.2f}'` °·s^-1^ (95% CI
[`{python} ci("bav_all_viso_par_ci_low", "bav_all_viso_par_ci_high", sign=True)`];
*t*(`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_par_df"]:.1f}'`) =
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_par_t"]:.2f}'`, *p* =
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_par_p"]:.3f}'`, *g* =
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_viso_par_g"]:.2f}'`).

Work per set was thus equated to within
`{python} f'{abs(S["bav_all_work_pct_bias"]):.1f}'`% of its grand mean and the
prescribed velocity delivered to within
`{python} f'{abs(S["bav_all_viso_pct_bias"]):.1f}'`% of its target, with
concordance correlation coefficients above 0.95 in both cases (Figure 5). Neither residual
bias is negligible in a statistical sense — both cell-level confidence intervals
exclude zero — but both are an order of magnitude smaller than the
between-modality differences reported in Section 2.2, and at the participant
level neither difference is distinguishable from zero.

The velocity result depends materially on excluding the dynamometer's ramps. If
isokinetic velocity is instead averaged over the whole repetition window, the
apparent NH − IK difference rises to
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_vwin_bias"]:+.2f}'` °·s^-1^
(`{python} f'{S["bav_all_vwin_pct_bias"]:+.2f}'`%), with limits of agreement of
`{python} sg("bav_all_vwin_loa_low")` to
`{python} sg("bav_all_vwin_loa_high")` °·s^-1^ lying entirely above zero and a
concordance correlation coefficient of
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_vwin_ccc"]:.3f}'`. The acceleration and deceleration
ramps account for `{python} f'{S["velphase_ramp_cost"]:.2f}'` of that
`{python} f'{S["bav_all_vwin_bias"]:.2f}'` °·s^-1^
(`{python} f'{100 * S["velphase_ramp_cost"] / S["bav_all_vwin_bias"]:.0f}'`%),
leaving the small residual reported above. Since the ramps are a property of the
apparatus and formed no part of the prescription, the whole-window figure
understates the fidelity with which the prescribed velocity was delivered.

Restricting both analyses to the analysed subset of repetitions changes two
things and should be read with the filter's known direction in mind
(Section 1.2). The work bias falls to
`{python} sg("bav_analysed_work_bias", 1)` J
(`{python} sg("bav_analysed_work_pct_bias")`%; 95% CI
[`{python} ci("bav_analysed_work_bias_ci_low", "bav_analysed_work_bias_ci_high", nd=1, sign=True)`],
*p* = `{python} f'{S["bav_analysed_work_bias_p"]:.3f}'`), and the velocity bias
to `{python} sg("bav_analysed_viso_bias")` °·s^-1^
(`{python} sg("bav_analysed_viso_pct_bias")`%) — but the velocity filter removes
precisely the repetitions that separate the groups, so this near-perfect
agreement is partly manufactured by the filter and is not independent
corroboration. Agreement remains excellent under both populations, which is the
substantive point.

## Time course of adaptation

**Discrete outcomes.** Mean and peak torque, knee range of motion, angle at peak
torque and mean knee angular velocity across the 15 training sessions are shown
in Figure 6. Linear mixed models retained all `{python} S["lmm_n_nh"]` NH and
`{python} S["lmm_n_ik"]` IK participants and used
`{python} n_cells` participant × session cells.

The largest between-modality difference was in the knee angle at which peak
torque occurred, which was markedly more flexed in the NH group
(`{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_nh"]`° versus
`{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_ik"]`°; estimated difference
`{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_est"]`°, 95% CI
[`{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_ci"]`],
*t*(`{python} S["lmmt_df"]`) = `{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_t"]`, *p*
`{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_p"]`), consistent with the regional
displacement of loading identified by the whole-curve analysis. Peak torque was
also higher in the NH group (`{python} d["peak_torque_nh"]` N·m versus
`{python} d["peak_torque_ik"]` N·m; difference `{python} d["peak_torque_est"]`
N·m [`{python} d["peak_torque_ci"]`], *t*(`{python} S["lmmt_df"]`) =
`{python} d["peak_torque_t"]`, *p* `{python} d["peak_torque_p"]`).

No between-group difference was observed for mean torque
(`{python} d["mean_torque_nh"]` N·m versus `{python} d["mean_torque_ik"]` N·m;
difference `{python} d["mean_torque_est"]` N·m [`{python} d["mean_torque_ci"]`],
*t*(`{python} S["lmmt_df"]`) = `{python} d["mean_torque_t"]`, *p*
`{python} d["mean_torque_p"]`) or for knee range of motion
(`{python} d["knee_ROM_nh"]`° versus `{python} d["knee_ROM_ik"]`°; difference
`{python} d["knee_ROM_est"]`° [`{python} d["knee_ROM_ci"]`],
*t*(`{python} S["lmmt_df"]`) = `{python} d["knee_ROM_t"]`, *p*
`{python} d["knee_ROM_p"]`). For mean knee angular velocity quantified over the
constant-velocity phase — the quantity the two modalities were matched on — the
groups did not differ meaningfully
(NH `{python} ms("lmmiso_knee_v_desc_nh_mean", "lmmiso_knee_v_desc_nh_sd")`
°/s versus IK
`{python} ms("lmmiso_knee_v_desc_ik_mean", "lmmiso_knee_v_desc_ik_sd")` °/s;
difference `{python} f'{S["lmmiso_knee_v_nhmik_est"]:+.2f}'` °/s, 95% CI
[`{python} ci("lmmiso_knee_v_ci_low", "lmmiso_knee_v_ci_high", sign=True)`],
χ^2^(`{python} S["lmmiso_knee_v_group_df"]`) =
`{python} f'{S["lmmiso_knee_v_group_chi2"]:.1f}'`, *p* =
`{python} f'{S["lmmiso_knee_v_group_p"]:.3f}'`), the interval including zero. A
model of the same form fitted to the whole-window velocity returns a difference
of the opposite sign (`{python} d["knee_v_mean_est"]` °/s
[`{python} d["knee_v_mean_ci"]`], *p* `{python} d["knee_v_mean_p"]`), which
reproduces at the level of the discrete outcomes the ramp artefact described
above. Neither estimate is robust: whichever velocity definition is used, the
group effect is the only one of the five that does not survive a correction for
the number of outcomes tested, and it should be read as no meaningful difference
rather than as a difference in either direction.

A significant main effect of time was observed for all five outcomes (angle at
peak torque χ^2^(`{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_time_df"]`) =
`{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_time_chi2"]`; peak torque
χ^2^(`{python} d["peak_torque_time_df"]`) =
`{python} d["peak_torque_time_chi2"]`; mean torque
χ^2^(`{python} d["mean_torque_time_df"]`) =
`{python} d["mean_torque_time_chi2"]`; knee range of motion
χ^2^(`{python} d["knee_ROM_time_df"]`) = `{python} d["knee_ROM_time_chi2"]`;
mean knee angular velocity χ^2^(`{python} S["lmmiso_knee_v_time_df"]`) =
`{python} f'{S["lmmiso_knee_v_time_chi2"]:.1f}'`; all *p* < 0.001), indicating
that both modalities produced changes across the training programme.

A group × time interaction was found for mean torque only
(χ^2^(`{python} d["mean_torque_interaction_df"]`) =
`{python} d["mean_torque_interaction_chi2"]`, *p*
`{python} d["mean_torque_interaction_p"]`); the interaction was not significant
for the angle at peak torque
(χ^2^(`{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_interaction_df"]`) =
`{python} d["angle_at_peak_torque_interaction_chi2"]`, *p* =
`{python} f'{S["lmm_angle_at_peak_torque_interaction_p"]:.3f}'`), peak torque
(χ^2^(`{python} d["peak_torque_interaction_df"]`) =
`{python} d["peak_torque_interaction_chi2"]`, *p* =
`{python} f'{S["lmm_peak_torque_interaction_p"]:.3f}'`), knee range of motion
(χ^2^(`{python} d["knee_ROM_interaction_df"]`) =
`{python} d["knee_ROM_interaction_chi2"]`, *p* =
`{python} f'{S["lmm_knee_ROM_interaction_p"]:.3f}'`) or mean knee angular
velocity (χ^2^(`{python} S["lmmiso_knee_v_interaction_df"]`) =
`{python} f'{S["lmmiso_knee_v_interaction_chi2"]:.1f}'`, *p* =
`{python} f'{S["lmmiso_knee_v_interaction_p"]:.3f}'`). The time course of
adaptation therefore differed between modalities for mean torque but not for the
remaining outcomes.

**Whole-curve progression.** Session-by-session comparisons of the torque curves
against the first training session are shown in Figure 6. With the per-comparison
α Bonferroni-corrected across the 14 comparisons, the IK group differed from
session 1 in `{python} S["prog_ik_bonf_n_sig"]` of
`{python} S["prog_n_comparisons"]` sessions, continuously from session
`{python} S["prog_ik_bonf_first_sustained"]` onwards, whereas the NH group did
so in `{python} S["prog_nh_bonf_n_sig"]` sessions (sessions
`{python} ", ".join(str(x) for x in S["prog_nh_bonf_sig_sessions"])`). Without
that correction the same contrast is significant in
`{python} S["prog_ik_unc_n_sig"]` of `{python} S["prog_n_comparisons"]` sessions
for the IK group, continuously from session
`{python} S["prog_ik_unc_first_sustained"]`, and in
`{python} S["prog_nh_unc_n_sig"]` sessions for the NH group, continuously from
session `{python} S["prog_nh_unc_first_sustained"]`.

Where torque increased, the increases were concentrated in the later portion of
the movement, and in the IK group the affected region widened progressively
across the programme. Under the corrected α, the final-session cluster in the IK
group extended from `{python} f'{S["prog_ik_bonf_tr15_start"]:.1f}'`% to
`{python} f'{S["prog_ik_bonf_tr15_end"]:.1f}'`% of the repetition
(*p* `{python} pv(S["prog_ik_bonf_tr15_p"])`, *n* =
`{python} S["prog_ik_bonf_tr15_n"]`), whereas **no cluster survived correction in
the NH group at the final session**. Without correction the corresponding
clusters were `{python} f'{S["prog_ik_unc_tr15_start"]:.1f}'`–`{python} f'{S["prog_ik_unc_tr15_end"]:.1f}'`%
in the IK group and
`{python} f'{S["prog_nh_unc_tr15_start"]:.1f}'`–`{python} f'{S["prog_nh_unc_tr15_end"]:.1f}'`%
in the NH group (*p* `{python} pv(S["prog_nh_unc_tr15_p"])`, *n* =
`{python} S["prog_nh_unc_tr15_n"]`). Two features of this analysis constrain its
interpretation: the number of participants contributing to each paired
comparison varied between 9 and 13 because both sessions had to be recorded for
a participant to be included, and the curves compared here are the three
repetitions of highest peak torque drawn from a pool that grows across the
programme, which inflates the apparent progression.
